Hippocampus, BG, and thalamus as supreme hubs

At the mesoscale, the cortex is a modular graph overlaid by a sparse, high-bandwidth core of hubs that are unusually well connected to one another-the "rich club.". These hub-to-hub edges are longer, thicker, and more heavily myelinated than average, so they are costly in wire and energy but buy global efficiency: a disproportionate fraction of shortest paths traverse the rich-club core, keeping average path length near  3 steps while most day-to-day traffic stays within modules 1, 2, 3. A game-theoretic model explains why robust brain-like communication networks accept efficiency costs (Figure) 11. Distributed hub networks trade communication efficiency for resilience to targeted failures (Figure).

Two hub classes matter computationally. "Connector hubs" have high participation coefficients: they bridge multiple modules and switch partners with task demands. Canonical examples include posterior cingulate/precuneus on the medial wall (DMN anchor with long temporal receptive windows), anterior insula and dorsal ACC (salience/control switches), lateral frontoparietal cortex (multiple-demand system), superior parietal/intraparietal areas (sensorimotor-attention nexus), and temporoparietal junction/anterior temporal cortex (semantic/conceptual convergence). "Provincial hubs" are highly connected within a module (e.g., early visual or auditory association zones) and stabilize local processing. Rich-club hubs are densely interlinked with each other (hub-hub "backbone") and spoke outward via major association tracts-the superior longitudinal/arcuate fasciculi (dorsal frontoparietal and language dorsal stream), inferior fronto-occipital and inferior longitudinal fasciculi (ventral object/semantic stream), uncinate (orbitofrontal-anterior temporal), and cingulum (medial wall DMN).

Dynamics reflect this geometry. Across primate cortex, feed-forward influences are preferentially expressed in faster gamma-band activity, whereas feedback/predictive signals are carried in slower alpha-beta rhythms; this frequency split is clearest in laminar recordings and inter-areal interactions along the visual hierarchy and generalizes to other cortices 4, 5. Inter-areal propagation times are on the order of a few to a few tens of milliseconds: the fastest callosal routes conduct in <5 ms, with many long cortico-cortical paths yielding effective delays of  3-20 ms that, together with synaptic and circuit latencies, set the phase relations that enable frequency-specific coupling across hubs 6, 7. Association-cortex hubs operate on longer intrinsic timescales-hundreds of milliseconds in single-unit and mesoscale measures-with network-level integration unfolding over seconds during naturalistic cognition, consistent with a temporal hierarchy from sensory to transmodal regions 8, 9, 10. In practice, the system behaves as a small-world, core-periphery network: segregated work is handled within modules and spokes, while brief, selective, frequency-aligned bursts through the rich-club backbone support global integration; "cortical architecture" therefore is a two-tier interconnect: many specialized spokes doing cheap, local computation, stitched together by a thin, expensive, and highly plastic core that enables rapid, goal-dependent integration across modalities, timescales, and cognitive domains.
